title: Why US Life Expectancy Lagged Behind Other Rich Nations

segments.label: scene 1 (title)
segments.text: The United States is the wealthiest major economy on Earth, producing $74,352 per person. Yet, its average life expectancy is just 79.3 years.

segments.label: scene 2 (slope)
segments.text: In the United Kingdom, GDP per person is lower at $53,423. Yet life expectancy there reaches 81.3 years.

segments.label: scene 3 (world_map)
segments.text: Japan tops the world's major economies, where people live to an average of 84.7 years.

segments.label: scene 4 (statement)
segments.text: Higher national wealth usually buys longer lives. But in America, that rule breaks down.

segments.label: scene 5 (countries_bars)
segments.text: Other peers pull ahead too. Australia sits at 83.9 years, France reaches 83.3 years, and Canada hits 82.6 years.

segments.label: scene 6 (multiline)
segments.text: In 1980, the US stood at 73.7 years, right alongside Germany's 73.1 years. But four decades of slower progress widened the gap.

segments.label: scene 7 (gauge)
segments.text: Despite reaching a high of 79.3 years in 2023, the American life span trails every comparable nation. Why?

segments.label: scene 8 (slope)
segments.text: Rewind four decades to 1980. Across the developed world, average lifespans clustered in a narrow band, according to data from Our World in Data.

segments.label: scene 9 (compare)
segments.text: In 1980, French citizens could expect to live to 74.2 years, showing how close European standards were at the time.

segments.label: scene 10 (line)
segments.text: Australia was virtually indistinguishable from its global peers, with an average life expectancy of 74.6 years in 1980.

segments.label: scene 11 (counter)
segments.text: Across the border, Canada held a slight lead among Western nations, recording an average lifespan of 75.1 years.

segments.label: scene 12 (gauge)
segments.text: Japan was already leading the industrial world, setting the upper baseline back in 1980 at 76.1 years.

segments.label: scene 13 (statement)
segments.text: America belonged squarely in this cohort. The United States started from the exact same baseline as its wealthiest global peers.

segments.label: scene 14 (multiline)
segments.text: This shared starting point set the stage for four decades of divergence, as peer nations steadily expanded their leads.

segments.label: scene 15 (bars)
segments.text: Over four decades, peer nations achieved remarkable gains in longevity. Australia expanded its average lifespan by +13% between 1980 and 2023.

segments.label: scene 16 (line)
segments.text: France achieved a +12% increase over those same decades, steadily widening its advantage through persistent health investments.

segments.label: scene 17 (compare)
segments.text: The United Kingdom also registered a +10% gain from 1980 to 2023, maintaining steady upward momentum.

segments.label: scene 18 (counter)
segments.text: In contrast, total lifespan growth in the United States managed just +8% over the entire period from 1980 to 2023.

segments.label: scene 19 (multiline)
segments.text: The sharpest deceleration occurred after 2010, when US life expectancy reached 78.7 years. From 2010 to 2023, overall change was a mere +1%.

segments.label: scene 20 (slope)
segments.text: During the crisis in 2020, American lifespans fell to 77.0 years. The subsequent +3% change through 2023 barely restored lost ground.

segments.label: scene 21 (statement)
segments.text: Four decades of slower gains turned a once tightly bound group into a persistent trailing position for America.

segments.label: scene 22 (statement)
segments.text: Multiple underlying causes drive America's health divergence. Chronic illness, unequal healthcare access, and substance abuse crises continuously pull lifespans down.

segments.label: scene 23 (world_map)
segments.text: Looking globally, average lifespans reveal extreme disparities. At the lowest end, Nigeria averages just 54.5 years in 2023.

segments.label: scene 24 (countries_bars)
segments.text: Nearby nations face similar severe challenges. Lifespans in Chad reach only 55.1 years.

segments.label: scene 25 (line)
segments.text: Conditions remain equally grim across other developing nations. Both Lesotho and the Central African Republic record average lifespans of 57.4 years.

segments.label: scene 26 (statement)
segments.text: In South Sudan, life expectancy stands at 57.6 years. Persistent poverty and fragile health infrastructure keep survival rates low.

segments.label: scene 27 (compare)
segments.text: By contrast, wealthy European peers sustained major health progress for decades. The United Kingdom reached a high of 81.4 years in 2019.

segments.label: scene 28 (slope)
segments.text: Wealthy democracies protected public health through broad medical access. Without equitable coverage and targeted care, national health outcomes inevitably slip.

segments.label: scene 29 (scatter)
segments.text: Does a stronger economy guarantee a longer life? Across 196 countries, wealth and longevity move together with a correlation of +0.75.

segments.label: scene 30 (statement)
segments.text: Money builds better sanitation, nutrition, and medical infrastructure. But once a nation reaches high income, extra economic output yields diminishing returns.

segments.label: scene 31 (kpi)
segments.text: Consider Japan, which reaches world-leading longevity while operating on a GDP per person of $47,387.

segments.label: scene 32 (scatter)
segments.text: France achieves outstanding health outcomes at a GDP per person of $54,297, while Canada delivers strong results at $58,088.

segments.label: scene 33 (kpi)
segments.text: Australia reaches a life expectancy of 83.9 years, while Germany reaches 81.4 years, proving peer nations convert prosperity into health efficiently.

segments.label: scene 34 (statement)
segments.text: Massive economic output fails to extend lives when care access is unequal and systemic health risks remain unaddressed.

segments.label: scene 35 (slope)
segments.text: Prosperity provides the foundation, but structural health investments ultimately decide whether high economic output translates into longer lives.

segments.label: scene 36 (statement)
segments.text: High national wealth creates the foundation for longevity, but money alone cannot protect public health. Converting economic prosperity into longer lives requires deliberate, systemic investment.

segments.label: scene 37 (line)
segments.text: Even during recent recovery years, American progress remained limited. From 2022 to 2023, United States life expectancy managed a +1.7% increase.

segments.label: scene 38 (line)
segments.text: By contrast, Japan consistently converted economic strength into lasting population health, increasing average lifespans by +9% from 1985 to 2023.

segments.label: scene 39 (bars)
segments.text: Over that same period, United States lifespan growth reached just +6% from 1985 to 2023, leaving a widening gap.

segments.label: scene 40 (statement)
segments.text: The key takeaway is straightforward. High GDP provides the tools, but universal access and preventative care determine whether a nation actually lives longer.
